title: Objects, copies, references, and pointers: links without unsafe memory
lead: Trace a live object through several access paths and distinguish changing an address from changing a value.
why: References and pointers enable shared access to objects. Their power requires a precise agreement about object existence, access paths, and valid lifetime. We begin with automatic objects without new/delete or pointer arithmetic.
objectives: Distinguish a value copy, reference, and pointer.
Read T&, T*, &object, and *pointer in context.
Check nullptr before access and account for lifetime.
Explain read-only access through const int* and const int&.
Draw symbolic links without relying on actual addresses.
prerequisites: Copying and assignment, scope and lifetime, bool, and simple if from Module 1.
The previous lesson’s expression distinctions and tracing one update at a time.

concepts.definition: In our declarations, an alias of an existing object; it needs initialization and cannot be reseated.
A separate object holding a pointer value, such as the address of a suitable live T or nullptr.
In &value, produces a pointer to the value object.
In *pointer, refers to the pointed-to object; access needs a valid pointer and valid lifetime.
A null pointer value; it must not be dereferenced.
A pointer whose former object has ended its lifetime; being non-null does not prove safe access.

sections.title: Session 1. Three relationships to a value
paragraphs: After int value{10};, int copy = value; creates an independent int. int& alias = value; creates a reference to the original object: alias is another way to refer to value, not a snapshot. alias = 12; changes value. Contrast this with lesson 5 copying.

In a declaration, & beside a type introduces a reference. In int* pointer = &value;, * beside the type declares a pointer and &value on the right obtains an address. Symbols have different roles in declarations and expressions; read the complete construct.

sections.title: A pointer is separate; an address is not a stock value
paragraphs: pointer holds a pointer value, while *pointer refers to the target object. *pointer = 15; changes value. pointer = &second; changes the pointer itself so access now leads to second. These are different operations and different state-journal events.

A diagram may name objects A and B and draw pointer → A. These are symbolic labels rather than numeric addresses. Actual addresses depend on the run, target, and environment and must not become expected stdout or stable learning-object identifiers.

sections.title: A reference is not reseated
paragraphs: After int& alias = first;, alias = second; copies second’s current value into first rather than switching the reference. selected = &second; really does reseat a pointer. Observe both original objects when testing or the distinction can remain invisible.

A reference is useful when access consistently names a known live object. A pointer can represent absence or selection, but does not by itself mean ownership. Neither references nor pointers here create or delete their targets.

sections.title: Session 2. nullptr and lifetime
paragraphs: int* selected{nullptr}; explicitly means no selected object. Check selected != nullptr before reading *selected. The familiar if/else chooses a safe branch: absent when null, or the value when present. This checks absence rather than proving every aspect of pointer validity.

A non-null pointer can dangle after its target leaves an inner block. Checking nullptr does not extend lifetime. Every dereference here targets a live object; null and dangling pointers are never dereferenced, even as a bad experiment. Record that data outlive all access paths in your project.

sections.title: const restricts a particular access path
paragraphs: const int* observer = &value; permits reading *observer but not changing value through this pointer. The original value can remain an ordinary int: value = 14; is valid and the observer sees 14. Likewise const int& view prohibits mutation through view. Read-only access does not imply that the source object can never change.

Do not remove const through a guessed cast to silence a diagnostic. The negative example deliberately requires a build rejection when writing through const int*. A constant pointer itself, int* const, can be studied later; the introductory contract focuses on const before int.

sections.title: An object journal and checks
paragraphs: In the laboratory, stock and snapshot are two objects; selectedStock references stock and stockPointer points to it. Subtracting 3 through the reference and adding 2 through the pointer gives 9 while the snapshot remains 10. Do not invent a separate stored-value object for selectedStock; the reference accesses stock.

Repeat the operations from initial values 3 and 20, safely within range. Explain the null example separately without forcing a crash. Preserve both a legend-labeled diagram and stdout: a picture alone does not prove execution, and stdout alone does not explain object relationships.

experiments.title: Assigning through a reference
experiments.action: Use first=5, second=9, int& alias=first; then alias=second;.
experiments.prediction: Both numbers become 9, but the reference still names first.
experiments.verification: Change second to 2 in a separate statement; first stays 9.

experiments.title: A shared object and a snapshot
experiments.action: Change initial value=10 to 20 while retaining later assignments to 12 and 15.
experiments.verification: Explain how copy records its creation-time value.

experiments.title: Presence instead of absence
experiments.action: In the null example declare int stock{6}; before selected and initialize selected=&stock.
experiments.prediction: Output becomes 6 instead of absent; stock is alive when read.
experiments.verification: Do not return a dead local object’s address or test dangling pointers by reading.

diagnostics.cause: Assignment through a reference changes the object.
diagnostics.fix: Use the explained pointer form when target selection is needed.
Establish the lifetime contract before access, without unsafe probe reads.

diagnostics.symptom: A const observer saw an updated value
diagnostics.cause: Read-only access was mistaken for source immutability.
diagnostics.fix: Distinguish object properties from access permissions.

practice.task: Draw value, copy, alias, and pointer after the first example.

practice.task: Reseat a pointer between two live ints and change only the second.
practice.criteria: The first stays unchanged, the second changes, and null is not read.

practice.task: Describe a non-owning selected-data contract: when it may be absent and how long it lives.
practice.criteria: Specify absence, checks, and lifetime without new/delete.
practice.hint: A non-null address alone is not proof.

laboratory.title: One stock object, several access paths
laboratory.challenge: Create a snapshot, reference, and pointer. Sell 3 through the reference and add 2 through the pointer. The snapshot must preserve its initial value.
rubric: The copy is not presented as an alias.
Provide a legend, values, and actual stdout.
No new/delete, pointer arithmetic, or unsafe reads.

assessment.question: What does *p=7 do for a valid int* p?
assessment.explanation: Indirection refers to the target object.

assessment.question: Does alias=second reseat int& alias=first?
answers: No, it copies the value into first
assessment.explanation: An ordinary reference is not reseated.

assessment.question: Does p!=nullptr prove the target is alive?
answers: No, lifetime needs a separate contract
assessment.explanation: A dangling pointer can remain non-null.

assessment.question: Can const int* observe a change to an ordinary source int?
answers: Yes, const restricts writes through this path
No, the source is frozen forever
assessment.explanation: Access-path properties differ from source-object properties.

reflection: Why can an address not be compared with one fixed expected number across runs?
What conditions beyond non-nullness are needed to read *p?
